claim: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis in budding yeast requires the formation of a dynamic actin network that produces the force to invaginate the plasma membrane against the intracellular turgor pressure.
source: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis in budding yeast requires the formation of a dynamic actin network that produces the force to invaginate the plasma membrane against the intracellular turgor pressure.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws on established knowledge about endocytosis in yeast and is supported by the experimental work in the paper.

claim: The type-I myosins Myo3 and Myo5 are important for endocytic membrane reshaping.
source: The type-I myosins Myo3 and Myo5 are important for endocytic membrane reshaping, but mechanistic details of their function remain scarce.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing effects of myosin deletion on membrane invagination.

claim: Type-I myosins promote, in a dose-dependent way, the growth and expansion of the actin network.
source: We show that the type-I myosins promote, in a dose-dependent way, the growth and expansion of the actin network, which controls the speed of membrane and coat internalization.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the quantitative data shown in Figures 1, 2, and 3, demonstrating dose-dependent effects of myosin levels on actin network assembly and invagination speed.

claim: Type-I myosins control the speed of membrane and coat internalization.
source: We show that the type-I myosins promote, in a dose-dependent way, the growth and expansion of the actin network, which controls the speed of membrane and coat internalization.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figures 1 and 3 showing that Sla1 inward movement speed correlates with myosin levels.

claim: Myosin activity is independent of the actin nucleation promoting activity of myosins.
source: We found that this myosin-activity is independent of the actin nucleation promoting activity of myosins, and cannot be compensated for by increasing actin nucleation.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 5 showing that deletion of the CA-domain (which has NPF activity) does not affect invagination speed, and Figure 6 showing that increasing actin nucleation by deleting BBC1 does not rescue the myo5Δ phenotype.

claim: Myosin activity cannot be compensated for by increasing actin nucleation.
source: We found that this myosin-activity is independent of the actin nucleation promoting activity of myosins, and cannot be compensated for by increasing actin nucleation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 6 showing that the myo5Δ bbc1Δ double mutant still has reduced invagination speed despite increased actin levels.

claim: Type-I myosins produce force by promoting actin filament polymerization.
source: Our results suggest a new mechanism for type-I myosins to produce force by promoting actin filament polymerization.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental data showing that myosins affect actin polymerization rates and invagination speed, but not through NPF activity.

claim: Endocytic membrane bending in budding yeast is strictly dependent on the assembly of a dynamic, branched actin network.
source: In budding yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) and fission yeast (Schizosaccharomyces pombe), endocytic membrane bending is strictly dependent on the assembly of a dynamic, branched actin network (Gachet and Hyams, 2005; Kaksonen et al., 2003), which is thought to provide the force to bend the membrane against the high turgor pressure of yeasts.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The actin network provides the force to bend the membrane against the high turgor pressure of yeasts.
source: In budding yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) and fission yeast (Schizosaccharomyces pombe), endocytic membrane bending is strictly dependent on the assembly of a dynamic, branched actin network (Gachet and Hyams, 2005; Kaksonen et al., 2003), which is thought to provide the force to bend the membrane against the high turgor pressure of yeasts.
evidence: This is a widely accepted model in the field, supported by citations.

claim: In metazoan cells, actin polymerization is required for clathrin-mediated endocytosis under conditions where the membrane resists bending.
source: In metazoan cells, actin polymerization is required for clathrin-mediated endocytosis under certain conditions where the membrane resists bending, for example in case of high membrane tension or strong substrate adhesion (Batchelder and Yarar, 2010; Boulant et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Actin filaments are nucleated through activation of the Arp2/3-complex, which induces the formation of new daughter filaments branching at a 70° angle from a mother filament.
source: Actin filaments are nucleated through activation of the Arp2/3-complex, which induces the formation of new daughter filaments branching at a 70° angle from a mother filament (Amann and Pollard, 2001a; Amann and Pollard, 2001b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Arp2/3 complex function, supported by citations.

claim: The main Arp2/3-activating nucleation promoting factors of budding yeast are Las17 and the type-I myosins Myo3 and Myo5.
source: The main Arp2/3-activating nucleation promoting factors (NPFs) of budding yeast, Las17 (homolog of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp)) and the type-I myosins Myo3 and Myo5, are recruited to a ring-shaped area on the plasma membrane surrounding the forming invagination, resulting in an inward flowing actin network (Idrissi et al., 2008; Mund et al., 2018; Picco et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Las17, Myo3, and Myo5 are recruited to a ring-shaped area on the plasma membrane surrounding the forming invagination, resulting in an inward flowing actin network.
source: The main Arp2/3-activating nucleation promoting factors (NPFs) of budding yeast, Las17 (homolog of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp)) and the type-I myosins Myo3 and Myo5, are recruited to a ring-shaped area on the plasma membrane surrounding the forming invagination, resulting in an inward flowing actin network (Idrissi et al., 2008; Mund et al., 2018; Picco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The actin network is connected to the tip of the invaginating membrane by the epsins and Sla2, proteins that bind both lipids and actin filaments.
source: This actin network is connected to the tip of the invaginating membrane by the epsins and Sla2, proteins that bind both lipids and actin filaments (Skruzny et al., 2015; Skruzny et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A large fraction of the force required to bend the membrane is provided by actin polymerization via a Brownian ratchet-type mechanism.
source: Though it is generally accepted that a large fraction of the force that is required to bend the membrane is provided by actin polymerization via a Brownian ratchet-type mechanism (Mogilner and Oster, 1996; Peskin et al., 1993), several modeling studies suggest that this force alone is not sufficient to counter the high turgor pressure of the cell (Carlsson and Bayly, 2014; Dmitrieff and Nédélec, 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the current understanding in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Modeling studies suggest that actin polymerization force alone is not sufficient to counter the high turgor pressure of the cell.
source: Though it is generally accepted that a large fraction of the force that is required to bend the membrane is provided by actin polymerization via a Brownian ratchet-type mechanism (Mogilner and Oster, 1996; Peskin et al., 1993), several modeling studies suggest that this force alone is not sufficient to counter the high turgor pressure of the cell (Carlsson and Bayly, 2014; Dmitrieff and Nédélec, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: Deletion of MYO5 resulted in a decrease in Sla1 inward movement speed from 26.2 ± 1.4 nm/s in WT cells to 17.1 ± 1.4 nm/s in myo5Δ.
source: Sla1 movement speed was reduced from 26.2 ± 1.4 nm/s (mean ± SE) in WT cells to 17.1 ± 1.4 nm/s in myo5Δ (p<0.001, Welch 2-sample t-test, see also Supplementary file 1 table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The growth rate of the membrane invagination is reduced in myo5∆ cells.
source: These data suggest that the growth rate of the membrane invagination is reduced in myo5∆ cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing reduced Sla1 and Sla2 movement speeds in myo5Δ cells.

claim: In myo5Δ the onset of Rvs167 assembly was delayed relative to the onset of Abp1 assembly.
source: In myo5Δ the onset of Rvs167 assembly was delayed relative to the onset of Abp1 assembly (Figure 1D, WT: 3.1 s, myo5Δ: 5.5 s).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In both myo5Δ and WT cells, Rvs167 was recruited once Sla2 reached an inward depth of ~45 nm.
source: However, in both myo5Δ and WT cells, Rvs167 was recruited once Sla2 reached an inward depth of ~45 nm (Figures 1C and 2A, WT: 39 ± 6 nm, myo5Δ: 47 ± 7 nm, p=0.381).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figures 1C and 2A.

claim: Rvs167 recruitment is triggered when the invagination reaches a certain length.
source: This suggests that Rvs167 recruitment is triggered when the invagination reaches a certain length.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Rvs167 is recruited at similar invagination depths in WT and myo5Δ despite different timing.

claim: In WT cells, the length of the accumulation period of Rvs167 molecules was 3.1 ± 0.1 s while in myo5Δ it was extended to 5.5 ± 0.3 s.
source: In WT cells, the length of the accumulation period of Rvs167 molecules was 3.1 ± 0.1 s (median ± SE, n = 103) while in myo5Δ it was extended to 5.5 ± 0.3 s (median ± SE, n = 29), resulting in similar peak amounts of Rvs167 molecules (peak number of molecules and standard error for WT: 136 ± 16, for myo5Δ: 110 ± 15, p=0.234).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The peak amounts of Rvs167 molecules are similar in WT and myo5Δ cells.
source: In WT cells, the length of the accumulation period of Rvs167 molecules was 3.1 ± 0.1 s (median ± SE, n = 103) while in myo5Δ it was extended to 5.5 ± 0.3 s (median ± SE, n = 29), resulting in similar peak amounts of Rvs167 molecules (peak number of molecules and standard error for WT: 136 ± 16, for myo5Δ: 110 ± 15, p=0.234).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Rvs167 molecules accumulated at a slower pace in myo5Δ cells.
source: Therefore, Rvs167 molecules accumulated at a slower pace in myo5Δ cells, in line with the hypothesis that the invagination growth rate is reduced in myo5Δ.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing extended accumulation period for Rvs167 in myo5Δ.

claim: At the moment when Rvs167 molecule numbers peaked, Sla2 had reached an inward depth of ~150 nm in both WT and myo5Δ.
source: At the moment when Rvs167 molecule numbers peaked (indicated by dashed and dotted vertical lines for WT and myo5Δ respectively), Sla2 had reached an inward depth of ~150 nm in both WT and myo5Δ (Figures 1C and 2A, WT: 145 ± 6 nm, myo5Δ: 169 ± 9 nm).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figures 1C and 2A.

claim: In myo5Δ the invagination growth rate is reduced, but since the growth phase is prolonged, similar final invagination lengths are reached.
source: Taken together these results indicate that in myo5Δ the invagination growth rate is reduced, but since the growth phase is prolonged, similar final invagination lengths are reached.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the data on Sla2 and Rvs167 dynamics.

claim: The assembly rates for all actin network proteins (Abp1, Cap1, Arc18, Sac6, Act1) were strongly reduced in myo5Δ cells as compared to WT cells.
source: We found that the assembly rates for all these proteins were strongly reduced in myo5Δ cells as compared to WT cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The durations of the accumulation periods for actin network proteins were extended by ~30% in myo5Δ, except for Arc18.
source: However, the durations of the accumulation periods were extended by ~30%, except for Arc18 for which the period was not prolonged.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Peak amounts of actin network proteins are comparable in WT and myo5Δ cells, except for Sac6 which was significantly reduced.
source: This resulted in comparable peak amounts of the actin network proteins in WT and myo5Δ cells (Figure 2D), except for Sac6 which was significantly reduced (p=0.018 vs WT).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There is a small but significant decrease (12%) in the amount of phalloidin per endocytic actin patch in myo5∆ cells.
source: We detected a small but significant decrease in the amount of phalloidin per endocytic actin patch in myo5∆ cells (12% decrease, p=0.022) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from phalloidin staining experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The absence of Myo5 resulted in a decrease in centroid movement speed for Act1, Abp1, Cap1 and Sac6, but not for Arc18.
source: The absence of Myo5 also resulted in a decrease in centroid movement speed for Act1, Abp1, Cap1 and Sac6, but not for Arc18 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Myo5 stimulates the addition of components to the growing actin network, leading to its expansion.
source: Taken together these results show that Myo5 stimulates the addition of components to the growing actin network, leading to its expansion.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the data on actin network assembly in myo5Δ cells.

claim: Myo3 and Myo5 started to assemble at the endocytic site at the same place and time.
source: Myo3 and Myo5 started to assemble at the endocytic site at the same place and time (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The accumulation rate was higher for Myo5, peaking at about twice as many Myo5 molecules than Myo3.
source: However, the accumulation rate was higher for Myo5, peaking at about twice as many Myo5 molecules than Myo3 (median number of molecules over the lifetime of the patch and standard error for Myo5: 77 ± 8, Myo3: 38 ± 4, p<0.001 in 1-sided z-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In myo3Δ Sla1 dynamics were similar to WT.
source: We imaged Sla1-EGFP in WT, myo3Δ and myo5Δ cells, and found that in myo3Δ Sla1 dynamics were similar to WT (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Myo5 recruitment is unaffected by the absence of Myo3.
source: We quantified Myo5-EGFP recruitment in myo3Δ cells and found it was unaffected by the absence of Myo3 (Figure 3D), nor was Myo3 recruitment increased when MYO5 was deleted.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Myo3 recruitment is not increased when MYO5 is deleted.
source: We quantified Myo5-EGFP recruitment in myo3Δ cells and found it was unaffected by the absence of Myo3 (Figure 3D), nor was Myo3 recruitment increased when MYO5 was deleted.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: On average 34% of the total pool of Myo3 molecules in the cell is located at endocytic sites, compared to 59% of Myo5 molecules.
source: We used these values to calculate that on average 34% of the total pool of Myo3 molecules in the cell is located at endocytic sites, compared to 59% of Myo5 molecules (see Materials and methods for calculations).
evidence: This is a calculation based on published cytoplasmic concentrations and measured recruitment levels.

claim: Myo5 has a higher affinity than Myo3 for endocytic sites.
source: Therefore, Myo5 has a higher affinity than Myo3 for endocytic sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calculation that a higher fraction of total Myo5 is at endocytic sites compared to Myo3.

claim: The numbers of protein molecules at endocytic sites in WT haploid and WT diploid cells were essentially identical.
source: First, we found that the numbers of protein molecules at endocytic sites in WT haploid and WT diploid cells were essentially identical, not only for myosins but also for two other endocytic proteins (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Myo3 and Myo5 recruitment were largely related to their gene dosage, and unaffected by the presence or absence of the other myosin paralog.
source: In general, Myo3 and Myo5 recruitment were largely related to their gene dosage, and unaffected by the presence or absence of the other myosin paralog.
evidence: This is a summary of the observations from the gene dosage experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Sla1 inward movement speed increased with higher total amounts of Myo3 and Myo5 in a dose-dependent way.
source: Intriguingly, we found that Sla1 inward movement speed increased with higher total amounts of Myo3 and Myo5 in a dose-dependent way (Figure 3E–G; Supplementary file 1 table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data shown in Figure 3E–G.

claim: Duplication of the MYO5 ORF in haploid cells resulted in a slight but significant increase in Sla1 inward movement speed to 30.6 ± 1.1 nm/s.
source: Duplication of the MYO5 ORF in haploid cells resulted in a slight but significant increase in Sla1 inward movement speed (Figure 3E, 30.6 ± 1.1 nm/s, p=0.011 vs WT).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There is a strong dose-dependent correlation between the number of myosin proteins at the endocytic site and the Sla1 inward movement rate.
source: To summarize, we found a strong dose-dependent correlation between the number of myosin proteins at the endocytic site, and the Sla1 inward movement rate (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a summary of the correlation shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Myosins control the speed of membrane invagination, potentially via controlling actin network growth.
source: This suggests that myosins control the speed of membrane invagination, potentially via controlling actin network growth.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the dose-dependent correlation between myosin levels and invagination speed.

claim: In Myo5-G132R cells, the Sla1-EGFP invagination movement was completely absent.
source: Consistently, we observed that in Myo5-G132R cells, the Sla1-EGFP invagination movement was completely absent (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: An average of ~40 Myo5-G132R molecules was recruited to endocytic sites.
source: An average of ~40 Myo5-G132R molecules was recruited to endocytic sites (Figure 4B), which is significantly less than the number of Myo5 molecules.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The motor activity is critical for the function of myosins in endocytic membrane invagination.
source: These data suggest that the motor activity is critical for the function of myosins in endocytic membrane invagination.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that the rigor mutant completely blocks invagination despite partial recruitment.

claim: Deletion of the CA-domain of Myo5 results in a slight decrease in the amount of Arc18 at endocytic sites.
source: Intriguingly we found a slight decrease in the amount of Arc18 at endocytic sites (Figure 5A, p=0.043 vs WT), similar to myo5Δ.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In myo5-CAΔ the amount of actin (Act1) was unchanged compared to WT.
source: However, while in myo5Δ the amount of actin (Act1) was strongly reduced, in myo5-CAΔ it was unchanged (Figure 5B, p=0.647 vs WT, p=0.001 vs myo5Δ).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Sla1 inward movement in myo5-CAΔ was essentially identical to WT.
source: Furthermore, Sla1 inward movement was essentially identical to WT, in contrast to the full MYO5 deletion (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The defects in actin network growth and invagination speed in the myo5Δ strains cannot be attributed to a decrease in NPF-activity.
source: This indicates that the defects in actin network growth and invagination speed in the myo5Δ strains cannot be attributed to a decrease in NPF-activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that deletion of the CA-domain does not affect invagination speed.

claim: Combining the deletions of MYO5 and BBC1 balanced out their opposing effects on actin nucleation, resulting in Act1 molecule numbers close to WT levels.
source: Combining the deletions of MYO5 and BBC1 balanced out their opposing effects on actin nucleation, resulting in Act1 molecule numbers that were close to WT levels (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Sla1 inward movement in myo5Δ bbc1Δ showed the combined phenotype of both single deletions: initially slowed down, but accelerated at later timepoints.
source: Intriguingly, Sla1 inward movement showed the combined phenotype of both single deletions: Sla1 centroid movement was initially slowed down, resembling myo5Δ, but accelerated at later timepoints, like in the bbc1Δ strain (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Although the additional deletion of BBC1 could compensate for the actin defect of myo5Δ, it was not sufficient to rescue invagination growth.
source: So although the additional deletion of BBC1 could compensate for the actin defect of myo5Δ, it was not sufficient to rescue invagination growth, suggesting that Myo5 has additional roles within the endocytic machinery besides the stimulation of actin filament nucleation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing that increased actin nucleation does not rescue the invagination defect.

claim: Myo5 has additional roles within the endocytic machinery besides the stimulation of actin filament nucleation.
source: So although the additional deletion of BBC1 could compensate for the actin defect of myo5Δ, it was not sufficient to rescue invagination growth, suggesting that Myo5 has additional roles within the endocytic machinery besides the stimulation of actin filament nucleation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that increasing actin nucleation does not rescue the myo5Δ phenotype.

claim: Deletion of MYO5 resulted in a slight but significant reduction in the outer radii of Abp1, Cap1, and Arc18.
source: However, deletion of MYO5 resulted in a slight but significant reduction in the outer radii of these proteins, indicating that the actin network on average was narrower.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the superresolution microscopy data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The actin network in myo5Δ is narrower than in WT.
source: However, deletion of MYO5 resulted in a slight but significant reduction in the outer radii of these proteins, indicating that the actin network on average was narrower.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the superresolution microscopy data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The myo5Δ dataset contained both invaginations and vesicles, indicating that productive scission had taken place.
source: The myo5Δ dataset contained both invaginations and vesicles, indicating that productive scission had taken place (Figure 8).
evidence: This is an observation from the CLEM data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The invaginations in myo5Δ had larger tip diameters than were reported for WT cells.
source: Intriguingly, the invaginations had larger tip diameters than were reported for WT cells (p=0.003, Figure 8C; Kukulski et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the CLEM data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The increase in invagination tip diameter in myo5Δ did not correlate with invagination length.
source: This increase did not correlate with invagination length (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), indicating that the expansion of the invagination tip is present throughout the whole invagination process.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myosin activity impacts the actin network architecture and endocytic membrane morphology.
source: Overall, these results indicate that myosin activity impacts the actin network architecture and endocytic membrane morphology.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the superresolution and CLEM data.

claim: Deletion or overexpression of one myosin paralog generally did not affect the recruitment of the other myosin paralog.
source: Deletion or overexpression of one myosin paralog generally did not affect the recruitment of the other myosin paralog, suggesting that at these expression levels Myo3 and Myo5 do not compete for binding sites.
evidence: This is a summary of the observations from the gene dosage experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At these expression levels Myo3 and Myo5 do not compete for binding sites.
source: Deletion or overexpression of one myosin paralog generally did not affect the recruitment of the other myosin paralog, suggesting that at these expression levels Myo3 and Myo5 do not compete for binding sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that deletion of one myosin does not increase recruitment of the other.

claim: The total number of recruited myosin molecules (Myo3 + Myo5) in MYO5-duplication strains was ~150 myosins.
source: Intriguingly, the total number of recruited myosin molecules (Myo3 + Myo5) in these two MYO5-duplication strains was the same at ~150 myosins, which may reflect the total number of available myosin binding sites within the endocytic machinery.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ~150 myosins may reflect the total number of available myosin binding sites within the endocytic machinery.
source: Intriguingly, the total number of recruited myosin molecules (Myo3 + Myo5) in these two MYO5-duplication strains was the same at ~150 myosins, which may reflect the total number of available myosin binding sites within the endocytic machinery.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation that total myosin recruitment plateaus at ~150 molecules.

claim: Scission is triggered once the invagination reaches a certain length, rather than after a set period of time.
source: All in all, we conclude that scission is triggered once the invagination reaches a certain length, rather than after a set period of time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Rvs167 is recruited at similar invagination depths in WT and myo5Δ despite different timing.

claim: Deletion of RVS167 results in shorter invaginations and smaller vesicles.
source: Note that deletion of RVS167 results in shorter invaginations and smaller vesicles (Kukulski et al., 2012a), indicating that scission of shorter invaginations is physically possible.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The absence of Myo5 results in a slowdown of nearly all aspects of endocytic vesicle budding, including actin network assembly and invagination elongation.
source: The absence of Myo5 results in a slowdown of nearly all aspects of endocytic vesicle budding, including actin network assembly and invagination elongation.
evidence: This is a summary of the observations from the various measurements in myo5Δ cells.

claim: At the crucial moment of scission, in myo5Δ most endocytic proteins have reached both similar amounts and positions as they would have in WT cells.
source: Therefore, at the crucial moment of scission, in myo5Δ most endocytic proteins have reached both similar amounts and positions as they would have in WT cells, suggesting that these modules are interconnected and/or respond to the membrane invagination state.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the data on protein dynamics in myo5Δ.

claim: Endocytic modules are interconnected and/or respond to the membrane invagination state.
source: Therefore, at the crucial moment of scission, in myo5Δ most endocytic proteins have reached both similar amounts and positions as they would have in WT cells, suggesting that these modules are interconnected and/or respond to the membrane invagination state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that proteins reach similar positions despite different timing in myo5Δ.

claim: The disassembly of the coat protein Sla1 is linked to the onset of actin assembly or membrane bending rather than scission.
source: Strikingly, the disassembly of the coat does not seem to be tightly connected to scission, as the disassembly of the coat protein Sla1 is linked to the onset of actin assembly or membrane bending rather than scission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Sla1 disassembly timing is different relative to scission in myo5Δ.

claim: At the time of scission in myo5Δ, Sla1 disassembly is nearly complete and will only continue for ~1.5 s, compared to ~3.7 s in WT cells.
source: At the time of scission in myo5Δ, Sla1 disassembly is nearly complete and will only continue for ~1.5 s, compared to ~3.7 s in WT cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the data.

claim: Premature coat disassembly can potentially explain the increased invagination tip diameter in myo5Δ.
source: This premature coat disassembly can potentially explain the increased invagination tip diameter we found in our myo5Δ CLEM dataset, as fewer coat proteins are present to maintain the diameter of the invagination tip.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting the observations of premature Sla1 disassembly and increased tip diameter.

claim: A similar expansion of invagination tip diameter was found in the sac6Δ strain and was attributed to fewer coat proteins being present.
source: A similar expansion of invagination tip diameter was also found in the sac6Δ strain, and was attributed to the same cause (Picco et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The actin network in myo5Δ is slightly but significantly narrower, which does not support the model that without myosins the actin network splays out over the plasma membrane surface.
source: However, our superresolution microscopy data showed the actin network in myo5Δ is slightly but significantly narrower (Figure 7), which does not support this model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the superresolution data in the context of a previously proposed model.

claim: Deletion of the Myo5 CA-domain has no effect on coat movement or Act1 accumulation, in contrast to the full deletion of MYO5.
source: Deletion of the Myo5 CA-domain has no effect on coat movement, nor on Act1 accumulation, in contrast to the full deletion of MYO5 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a summary of the observations from Figure 5.

claim: Deletion of Myo3 and Myo5 CA-domains has no effect on cell growth.
source: This is in line with previous studies showing that the deletion of Myo3 and Myo5 CA-domains has no effect on cell growth (Evangelista et al., 2000; Lechler et al., 2000), endocytic internalization (Galletta et al., 2008; Geli et al., 2000), or actin patch motility as measured by mean-square-displacement (Galletta et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deletion of Myo3 and Myo5 CA-domains has no effect on endocytic internalization.
source: This is in line with previous studies showing that the deletion of Myo3 and Myo5 CA-domains has no effect on cell growth (Evangelista et al., 2000; Lechler et al., 2000), endocytic internalization (Galletta et al., 2008; Geli et al., 2000), or actin patch motility as measured by mean-square-displacement (Galletta et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deletion of Myo3 and Myo5 CA-domains has no effect on actin patch motility as measured by mean-square-displacement.
source: This is in line with previous studies showing that the deletion of Myo3 and Myo5 CA-domains has no effect on cell growth (Evangelista et al., 2000; Lechler et al., 2000), endocytic internalization (Galletta et al., 2008; Geli et al., 2000), or actin patch motility as measured by mean-square-displacement (Galletta et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myo3 and Myo5 stimulate actin filament polymerization rather than nucleation.
source: Taken together our results indicate that Myo3 and Myo5 stimulate actin filament polymerization rather than nucleation.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the data showing that NPF activity is not required for myosin function and that increasing nucleation does not rescue the phenotype.

claim: The polymerization rate of single actin filaments and complex networks decreases with increasing loads, until growth completely stalls.
source: The polymerization rate of single actin filaments (Footer et al., 2007) and of complex networks (Bieling et al., 2016) decreases with increasing loads, until growth completely stalls.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is a large gap between the required force to deform the plasma membrane in yeast and the force an endocytic actin network could produce.
source: In recent years, estimates have been made for both the force required to deform the plasma membrane in yeast (Dmitrieff and Nédélec, 2015), and for the amount of force an endocytic actin network could produce (Berro et al., 2010; Carlsson and Bayly, 2014; Zhang et al., 2015), revealing a large gap between the required and produced forces, suggesting that the endocytic ratchet should fail.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: Type-I myosins increase the polymerization rate of actin filaments by decreasing the load on their tips.
source: Based on our results, we propose a working model where type-I myosins increase the polymerization rate of actin filaments by decreasing the load on their tips (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Myosins could reorient actin filaments facing the plasma membrane, either by pushing them inwards or by rotating them away from the membrane, allowing their further elongation.
source: Myosins could reorient actin filaments facing the plasma membrane, either by pushing them inwards or by rotating them away from the membrane, allowing their further elongation, resulting in actin network growth.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic proposal based on the experimental findings.

claim: Myosins essentially function as an actin polymerase: they facilitate the addition of new actin monomers to existing filaments under conditions of high loads.
source: In our working model, myosins essentially function as an actin polymerase: they facilitate the addition of new actin monomers to existing filaments under conditions of high loads, thereby allowing actin network growth.
evidence: This is a proposed functional model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Deletion of both MYO3 and MYO5 results in a complete block in endocytosis.
source: Previous studies have shown that deletion of both MYO3 and MYO5 results in a complete block in endocytosis (Geli and Riezman, 1996; Goodson et al., 1996; Sun et al., 2006), making it difficult to narrow down how these proteins contribute to each subsequent phase of the endocytic process.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myo3 and Myo5 are highly similar and functionally redundant.
source: The budding yeasts type-I myosins Myo3 and Myo5 are highly similar and functionally redundant.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these proteins, supported by the experimental observations in the paper.

claim: Deletion of both Myo3 and Myo5 leads to a complete block in endocytosis and a severe growth defect.
source: Deletion of both Myo3 and Myo5 leads to a complete block in endocytosis and a severe growth defect, while single deletions result in no or only very minor defects in endocytosis only under heat stress conditions, and show no growth phenotype (Anderson et al., 1998; Geli and Riezman, 1996; Goodson et al., 1996; Goodson and Spudich, 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Single deletions of MYO3 or MYO5 result in no or only very minor defects in endocytosis only under heat stress conditions, and show no growth phenotype.
source: Deletion of both Myo3 and Myo5 leads to a complete block in endocytosis and a severe growth defect, while single deletions result in no or only very minor defects in endocytosis only under heat stress conditions, and show no growth phenotype (Anderson et al., 1998; Geli and Riezman, 1996; Goodson et al., 1996; Goodson and Spudich, 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myo5 has been shown to have motor activity in vitro.
source: Myo5 has been shown to have motor activity in vitro (Sun et al., 2006), and Myo3 and Myo5 rigor mutants - which bind to actin filaments but cannot release them - block endocytic internalization (Lechler et al., 2000; Lewellyn et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Myo3 and Myo5 rigor mutants block endocytic internalization.
source: Myo5 has been shown to have motor activity in vitro (Sun et al., 2006), and Myo3 and Myo5 rigor mutants - which bind to actin filaments but cannot release them - block endocytic internalization (Lechler et al., 2000; Lewellyn et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myo5's TH1-domain has been shown to bind to phospholipids in vitro.
source: Myo5's TH1-domain has been shown to bind to phospholipids in vitro (Fernández-Golbano et al., 2014) and is required for efficient recruitment of Myo5 to endocytic sites (Grötsch et al., 2010; Lewellyn et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myo5's TH1-domain is required for efficient recruitment of Myo5 to endocytic sites.
source: Myo5's TH1-domain has been shown to bind to phospholipids in vitro (Fernández-Golbano et al., 2014) and is required for efficient recruitment of Myo5 to endocytic sites (Grötsch et al., 2010; Lewellyn et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Myo5 SH3-domain interaction with Vrp1 is essential for recruitment of Myo5 to endocytic sites.
source: Myo5 SH3-domain interaction with Vrp1 is essential for recruitment of Myo5 to endocytic sites (Lewellyn et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The CA-domain of Myo5 together with Vrp1 possess NPF-activity in vitro.
source: Finally, the CA-domain together with Vrp1 possess NPF-activity in vitro (Evangelista et al., 2000; Galletta et al., 2012; Galletta et al., 2008; Geli et al., 2000; Lechler et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both Myo3 and Myo5 CA-domains can be deleted without affecting endocytosis.
source: Myo3 and Myo5 were initially presumed to act mainly as NPFs (Evangelista et al., 2000; Giblin et al., 2011), however both their CA-domains can be deleted without affecting endocytosis (Galletta et al., 2008), indicating that Myo3 and Myo5 have additional functions within the endocytic machinery.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Myo3 and Myo5 have additional functions within the endocytic machinery beyond NPF activity.
source: Myo3 and Myo5 were initially presumed to act mainly as NPFs (Evangelista et al., 2000; Giblin et al., 2011), however both their CA-domains can be deleted without affecting endocytosis (Galletta et al., 2008), indicating that Myo3 and Myo5 have additional functions within the endocytic machinery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CA-domain deletion does not affect endocytosis, supported by citation.

claim: Transiently lowering the force requirements can rescue the endocytic defects of Myo1 deletion in fission yeast.
source: This is in line with observations that transiently lowering the force requirements can rescue the endocytic defects of Myo1 deletion in fission yeast (Basu et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In WT cells, invaginations grow up to ~150 nm long before scission occurs, resulting in the release of a 60 nm long, ellipsoidal vesicle.
source: In WT cells, invaginations grow up to ~150 nm long before scission occurs, resulting in the release of a 60 nm long, ellipsoidal vesicle (Idrissi et al., 2008; Kukulski et al., 2012a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Membrane scission coincides with the disassembly of the BAR-scaffold from the invagination neck.
source: Membrane scission coincides with the disassembly of the BAR-scaffold from the invagination neck (Picco et al., 2015), but the causal relationship between these two observations remains unknown.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The distribution of invagination lengths is not affected by the absence of Myo5.
source: Finally, the CLEM dataset shows that the distribution of invagination lengths is not affected by the absence of Myo5 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the CLEM data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cytoplasmic concentrations of Myo3 and Myo5 have been reported as 152 nM and 172 nM respectively.
source: The cytoplasmic concentrations of Myo3 and Myo5 have been reported as 152 nM and 172 nM respectively (Boeke et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.
